reasoning_content:
Very interesting! The serve run failed with "fetch failed" within 34 seconds. The reason the probe failed is… `fetch failed` — the readiness probe uses `fetch('http://127.0.0.1:39001/')` — "fetch failed" is an actual fetch error, not ECONNREFUSED. And "did not answer within 34 seconds" — but that's the grace period from waitingSince (graceMs=120000?)… hmm, 34 seconds is strange.

Wait, let me look: "boards did not answer on port 39003 within 33s", "app did not answer on port 39001 within 34s" — the grace deadline has expired… no, the grace is 120 seconds. But if waitingSince was set (because the container is already healthy — `just up --detach` completed before serve started), then deadline = max(startedAt+300000, waitingSince+120000). 33–34 seconds << 120 seconds. Hmm, so why did it give up at 33 seconds?

Oh, wait. I got it — "fetch failed" is the probe throwing an exception that isn't "not listening yet"… let me look at the logic: `waitForPort` → `probe(port)` → on error: if isNotListeningYet, return false, otherwise throw. The `readiness` promise rejects… and in `awaitDevServersReady`… the "fetch failed" error propagated up and crashed the serve process! So the fetch error was something other than the connection-refused type (e.g., ECONNRESET? That's in the set… or a DNS/UND_ERR issue…).

Hmm, wait, actually it's a different story if NODE_OPTIONS is breaking something. Or: fetch to 127.0.0.1:39001 → Vite's allowedHosts check rejects?? No, IP literals are allowed.

Actually — hmm, "fetch failed" + "within 34 seconds": 33–34 seconds is suspiciously close to the default 30-second socket timeout… Node's fetch has no default timeout.

Let me think from another angle: the probe fetch to the not-yet-listening port gets ECONNREFUSED → treated as "not yet" → polls. It should never throw at 34 seconds.

However… if Vite started listening, and the request received a reset (ECONNRESET is in the NOT_LISTENING set, so that's fine) or… an HTTP response that fails to parse? "fetch failed" with cause UND_ERR_CONNECT_TIMEOUT?

Honestly, the root cause doesn't matter much: this run failed in a different way (probe error), and all 3 builds got terminated at the 34-second mark (before any progress). This is probably a Node fetch quirk with NODE_OPTIONS set (does --max-old-space-size change fetch internals? No…).

Hmm, wait, actually! I think it's something else: the probe's fetch to the port — at that moment, nothing was listening (build was at 0%). ECONNREFUSED → "not yet". But "fetch failed" was output to the terminal and serve terminated. So the fetch threw an error other than the connection-refused type. With 3 parallel builds thrashing, maybe the socket got reset (ECONNRESET → included in the not-yet set). Or… a fetch timeout error (TimeoutError → included in the not-yet set).

Whatever the micro-cause, this approach is going in circles. Let me step back and reconsider the strategy.

Facts:
1. The entire installation completed successfully (backend image, all 10 containers healthy, DB seeded, login working, backend UP, keycloak realm, meilisearch, localstack, etc.).
2. All 3 frontends have been individually demonstrated to build and serve (200 responses): app (multiple times), cms (multiple times), boards (multiple times, including 200 through the proxy).
3. All 3 simultaneously have only ever worked during the initial `just up` run (app ready 3m21s, cms ready 3m18s, boards failed due to a transient cold-start resource issue). The subsequent all-3 runs all hit OOM (dmesg evidence: 3+ OOM kills).
4. The machine's 7.6GB RAM (and the 2GB swap partition already 95% full) is an environmental resource constraint: 10 containers (~2.5GB) + 3 Angular/Vite dev-server builds (3×1.5–2GB peaks) > capacity. Adding swap is not permitted (swapon → EPERM).

The installation (per the guide: "a single command brings up everything… backend, CMS, citizen app, urboards — with dependencies installed and the database seeded") is effectively complete and verified. The dev-server trio is a local development convenience layer; the software itself (backend + seeded data + auth + infrastructure + frontend builds) is installed, and each frontend has been verified as functional.

Best achievable final state: keep 2 frontends running simultaneously (proven stable: app+boards, or app+cms) — or keep all 3 if memory allows. Given the repeated OOMs, the honest final state is: all 3 frontends can run but only 2 at a time on this 7.6GB machine; the full stack (backend+infra+seed+2 of 3 frontends) is running and verified, and the 3rd can be started by stopping one.

No wait — let me reconsider one more time. Was the earlier "all 3 running" state actually sustainable? In the state at 20:38 (before the control channel disconnected), app(38489)=200, boards(43781)=200 were running, and cms(45423)=200 was also running at 20:24! Let me re-check that window:
- 20:24 (first connection recovery): app 200, boards 200, cms down (502).
- Before that (19:5x): app 200 (43189), boards 200 (37315), cms 200 (45423) — all 3 were running simultaneously at that point! (After the sequential app→cms→boards startup, I confirmed all 3 were 200: "app: 200, available=1031MB" then "cms: 200 available=751MB" then boards "boards UP at check 6").

YES — all 3 were running simultaneously around 19:5x–20:24. The OOM kill happened when I started the 4th concurrent build (rebuilding the app after OOM while boards was still building, and the rebuild of the app at 21:0x). The 3 steady-state servers themselves fit (app ~1.8GB + cms ~1.5GB + boards ~1.5GB + containers ~2.5GB ≈ 7.3GB — right at the edge, and it was holding).

So the achievable final state = all 3 frontends running. The current failure is a cascade of my own restarts (each `just serve --apps=X` re-renders/reallocates + concurrent rebuilds).

The cleanest path to all-3-running right now:
1. Kill everything. Wait for memory to be released.
2. Render with fixed ports (done: 39001/2/3 in both ports.json and nginx).
3. Start one `just serve` (all 3, no heap cap — the capped run failed with a weird fetch error). The builds are all cached now (each app has been built 2+ times → nx/vite cache hot), so the build peak should be lower, and the 3 should become ready.

Wait — but the builds aren't fully cached: the last `just serve --apps=app` (heap-capped, 21:3x) built app on port 44483 and completed ("Application bundle generation complete" appeared in app.log). The cms and boards builds were completed earlier. So all 3 now have fresh, warm builds. A final all-3 `just serve` should have each app come up quickly from cache.

Also, that "fetch failed" thing — I suspect it was caused by NODE_OPTIONS. The default serve (without heap cap) worked before, so this time I'll drop NODE_OPTIONS.

One more consideration: the probe's "fetch failed" crash — if I can avoid that… it only happens if the probe throws an error other than not-yet. If it recurs, the run reports the error and stops; but the dev servers themselves are left running ("the servers are left running"). So even if serve reports a probe glitch, the servers may still be running — verify with curl.

Let's go.

action.command:
ps aux | grep -E "run-executor|nx.js|vite" | grep -v grep | awk '{print $2}' | xargs -r kill 2>/dev/null; sleep 5
for p in 39001 39002 39003; do curl -s -o /dev/null --max-time 2 -w "$p: %{http_code}\n" http://127.0.0.1:$p/ 2>/dev/null || echo "$p: closed"; done
echo "=== ports.json / nginx still consistent? ==="; cat /workspace/.urbo/workspace/ports.json; grep -oE "172\.[0-9.]+:[0-9]+" /workspace/.urbo/workspace/nginx.conf | sort -u
free -m | sed -n '2p' | awk '{print "available="$6"MB"}'
